Hebrew יהודהder.

Yiddish ייִדיש
From Middle High German jüdesch, from Old High German judeisc, derived from judo, judeo + -isc, the former from Latin iūdaeus (“Judaean, Jew”), from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαῖος (Ioudaîos), derived from Ἰουδά (Ioudá, “Judah”) + -ιος (-ios), the former from Hebrew יְהוּדָה (yəhūḏāh). By surface analysis, ייִד (yid) + ־יש (-ish).

etymology_text: Unknown. Started appearing in Eastern Yiddish dialects from the 16th century. Several etymologies were proposed: from Romance, related to Latin dīvīnus or to Old French deviner (“to wish”). Another possible Romance explanation would connect davenen with a Judeo-Romance stem related to Old French devoer/devouer “to devote, consecrate” < Latin devovere. On this view, the form would have been Germanized with the Yiddish infinitive ending -en, comparable to Western Yiddish oren/orn “to pray” < Romance orer/orare. Another proposed etymology links the verb to Middle High German dœnen, although this raises several phonological problems. Finally, the verb was linked to Hebrew דבר (dāvar, “to speak”).

etymology_text:
Since there is no apparent Hebrew, Germanic, or Slavic source for it, scholars have looked for a Romance provenance and come up with two possibilities: one is Ancient Greek Φοῖβος (Phoîbos), a word meaning “bright” or “shining,” used by the ancient Greeks as an epithet for the god Apollo, perhaps through Latin Phoebus. Although nothing like it can be found in ancient Jewry, we come across it in the 17th century, when well-known Polish rabbi Shmuel ben Uri Shraga Faybish (or Fayvush) spelled his name “Phoebus” in Latin characters, as did his descendants. Further strengthening the case for it is the frequent Eastern European combination Shraga-Fayvush (or Fayvl), since "shraga" means “light” in the Aramaic of the Talmud. See שְׁרָגָא (shraga), a cognate of Arabic سِرَاج (sirāj) and Classical Syriac ܫܪܓܐ (shraga). Jews often gave children double names, joining Hebrew-Aramaic ones to parallel ones in the local language, and Shraga-Fayvush might be the Yiddish form of an earlier Mediterranean Jewish doublet that has been lost. The Hebrew name אורי ("Uri"), it should be pointed out, comes from אור ("or"), which means “light,” too.
Yet an alternate theory holds that Fayvush-Fayvl descends from Latin vivus (“living”), which we also find translated into Hebrew as חיים (hayyim), and that the spelling of “Phoebus” is a 17th-century affectation. A Jewish family called Vives can be found in 12th-century Barcelona, and the name existed among other Spanish Jews. And for that matter, consider also the possibility that Fayvush/Fayvl comes from the Roman name Fabius, from Latin Fabius, or its Italian form, from Old Italian Fabio.

head_templates.expansion: שמאָק • (shmok) m, plural שמעק (shmek), diminutive שמעקל (shmekl)

etymology_text:
Uncertain, with several proposed possibilities:
* Possibly from Old Polish smok (“dragon”) or Bulgarian смок (smok, “grass snake”). Perhaps akin to onomatopoeic Russian смоктать (smoktatʹ, “to suck”) according to old belief that snakes suck milk from animals.
* Or from Old Polish ćmok (“dim lighted”),
* Alternatively a baby-talk corruption of שמעקל (shmekl), a dissimilated form of שטעקל (shtekl, “penis/willy”, literally “little stick”).
* Alternatively from Middle High German smucken, archaic German schmucken, which has several meanings respectively allowing different semantic connections: “to squeeze, press, fit into something tight”; “to hug, snuggle, kiss”; “to adorn, decorate”. (The last of these senses is less likely, but compare German Schmuck (“jewellery”) and English crown jewels.)

etymology_text: From Middle High German pfërsich, from Old High German phërsih, early borrowing (before CE 700) from Medieval Latin persica (“peach (fruit)”). The Yiddish form is phonetically regular with the exception of the last syllable, which has been assimilated to the suffix ־קע (-ke). Similar forms exist in some dialects of East Central German; they are probably due to association of final -ich with the ending at hand in ־יק (-ik), which is pronounced /ɪk/ in Yiddish, but /ɪç/ in many adjacent dialects of German. Compare German Pfirsich, Dutch perzik. See also English peach for more.

etymology_text:
An expansion of earlier *לייען (*leyen) (still attested in Alsace as [ˈlaːjə], [(ɡə)ˈlaːɪ̯t]) + ־ען (-en), from a Romance language, from Latin legere (“to read”).
The precise donor language is uncertain. Old French, the likeliest candidate by default, offers phonetic difficulties, but perhaps from leire, early byform of lire. Northern Italian forms like Friulian lei have been invoked alternatively. However, it must be noted that Yiddish -ey- regularly develops from earlier [eː], meaning that Old Spanish leer is just as plausible.

etymology_text:
Probably from Middle High German bruch (“breach, breaking, fracture”), from Old High German bruh, from Proto-Germanic *brukiz, an
ablaut derivation from *brekaną, whence ברעכן (brekhn, “to break”). Cognate with German Bruch, Dutch breuk, English breach. The unexpected Yiddish -o- (instead of -u-) would have been influenced by the past participle געבראָכן (gebrokhn, “broken”).
Alternatively it might continue a closely related Old High German broh (“broken-off piece”), from Proto-Germanic *brukaz. Cognate with Dutch brok, Old English (ge)broc. However, this word appears not to be attested anymore in Middle High German and the Yiddish sense is closer to the above-mentioned bruch.

etymology_text:
From Middle High German soldener (“mercenary, sellsword”), soldner or soldenære, derived from Medieval Latin soldarius. Appears to have undergone a semantic shift from "mercenary" to "soldier", perhaps under influence from Polish żołnierz (“soldier, private”).
Compare also modern German Söldner (“mercenary, sellsword”), Slovak žoldnier (“mercenary”), Czech žoldnéř (“mercenary”).

etymology_text:
From Old High German chintpetti and similar forms, whence also German Kindbett (“childbirth, bed of childbirth”).
Old High German chintpetti consists of chint (“child”) (whence German Kind, Yiddish קינד (kind)) and petti (“bed”) (whence German Bett, Yiddish בעט (bet)). By surface analysis, קינד (kind) + בעט (bet).

examples.english: At night, he would count up his profits and get angry that people didn't pay him, or that didn't have enough to pay off the outstanding notes, and even in sleep, he would dream about flour, about grains.

examples.english: He dreamed of running a large beth-midrash and delivering profound Musar talks.

etymology_text: From Middle High German narre, from Old High German narro (“fool, idiot, clown, stupid or crazy person”). Further origin unknown. etymology_text: Probably from Middle High German siu, a byform of sie (“she, they”), whence Yiddish זי (zi, “she”). Originally siu was nominative feminine and plural neuter, while sie was accusative feminine and plural masculine/feminine. This distinction was lost altogether in Standard German. However, systems that have made sie the feminine form and siu the plural form do exist in certain varieties of Bavarian. The Yiddish outcome of siu should actually be *zay rather than zey, but minor phonetic deviations are not unusual in function words.

etymology_text:
From Middle High German sich, from Old High German sih, from Proto-Germanic *sik, which see for cognates.
Some German dialects use sich as a general reflexive of the plural. This usage clearly started out from the Middle High German accusative variant unsich (“us, ourselves”), as it is more widespread for the 1st person plural than the 2nd person. However, no dialect seems to allow sich for the 1st and 2nd persons singular. At least this part of the Yiddish development was most likely influenced by descendants of Proto-Slavic *sę, *sebe.

glosses: Reflexive pronoun for all persons and numbers: itself, himself, herself, oneself, themselves, myself, ourselves, yourself, yourselves.

etymology_text: Borrowed from German Liebe (“love”), from Middle High German liebe (“joy, affection, kindliness”), from Old High German lioba, liobī, derived from the adjective liob (whence Yiddish ליב (lib)), from Proto-Germanic *leubaz, from Proto-Indo-European *lewbʰ- (“love, care, desire”). The sense “(romantic) love” developed only in early modern German, replacing older Minne; the noun as such is absent from many German dialects. The final -e in Yiddish also attests to the non-native origin.

etymology_text: Middle High German did not have an s-plural. The Yiddish form probably comes from a confluence of two origins: The use after unstressed -e corresponds to Hebrew ־ות (-ôṯ), which is pronounced [əs] in Yiddish (and Ashkenazi Hebrew). The use after unstressed sonorants is very similar to Middle Low German and likely influenced by it. Compare German -s (also from Middle Low German), English -s (inherited).

examples.text: Finally, khavershaft highlighted internal networks of trust and solidarity that were important underpinnings of communities, especially for Bundist immigrants.
examples.ref: 2024, Naomi Hemstreet, “Jewish Immigrants in Argentina: The Bund as a Transnational Connection”, in Young Historians Conference (in English), page 5:

examples.text: However, self-assertion in an increasingly anti-Semitic climate was possible only through the strong internal coherence of the Bundist meshpokhe (family), which comprised a complex community of Jews from all walks of life – a community characterized by strong convictions and solidarity. The meshpokhedikeyt was apparently a trade mark of the Bund for contemporaries, too. However, meshpokhedikeyt and khavershaft (comradeship) did not mean that there were no conflicts. As in any proper family, there were repeated ‘family fights’ within the Bund – top–down between the party leadership and the party base, and horizontally between the moderate party majority, the Eynser, and the boisterous left wing, the Tsveyer. Nevertheless, internal conflicts were conducted in the context of a highly developed political culture of reflection and controversy, probably unprecedented in the history of political parties in the twentieth century.
examples.ref: 2016, Dieter Gosewinkel, Dieter Rucht, Gertrud Pickhan, chapter 5, in Transnational Struggles for Recognition: New Perspectives on Civil Society since the 20th Century (in English), page 164:

examples.roman: tsienizm iz an idyologye vos halt az yidn in moderne tsaytn zoln zikh umkern tsu dem historishe land fun di yidn, erets yisroel.
examples.translation: Zionism is an ideology that holds that Jews in modern times should return to the historical land of the Jews, the Land of Israel.

examples.text: אין סאָװעטן־פֿאַרבאַנד איז ייִדיש דערקלערט געװאָרן ווי „די‟ ייִדישע שפּראַך, אַנטקעגן העברעיִש, װאָס איז געװאָרן טריף־פּסול װי די שפּראַך פֿון רעליגיע און ציוניזם.
examples.ref: 2020 April 24, Mikhail Krutikov, “װי פּאָליטיש זײַנען ייִדישע לימודים?”, in Forverts:
examples.english: In the Soviet Union Yiddish was declared to be “the” Jewish language, opposed to Hebrew, which became anathema as the language of religion and Zionism.
examples.roman: in sovetn-farband iz yidish derklert gevorn vi „di‟ yidishe shprakh, antkegn hebreish, vos iz gevorn treyf-posl vi di shprakh fun religye un tsienizm.

etymology_text:
From Middle High German blōȥ (“naked, bare, unarmed, exposed, wretched”), from Old High German blōz, from Proto-Germanic *blautaz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰlaw- (“weak, frightened”). Cognate with German bloß (“naked, mere, sole”), Dutch bloot (“bare, naked”), Swedish blott (“merely, just”).
The sense “dull” can be derived from “unarmed”. The sense “stupid” can be derived thence or even from “naked” directly; compare German bloßstellen (“to embarrass, stultify”). Therefore influence by Middle High German blœde (“frail, craven”), whence German blöd (“stupid”), is not absolutely necessary, although it does appear likely and would also explain the front vowel in the variant bleyz above.

examples.text:
Rozhinkes mit Mandlen (Yiddish folk lullaby):
אונטער ייִדעלע׳ס וויגעלע / שטייט אַ קלאָר־ווײַס ציגעלע. / דאָס ציגעלע איז געפֿאָרן האַנדלען. / דאָס וועט זײַן דײַן באַרוף, / ראָזשינקעס מיט מאַנדלען. / שלאָף־זשע, ייִדעלע, שלאָף.
unter yidele's vigele / shteyt a klor-vays tsigele. / dos tsigele iz geforn handlen. / dos vet zayn dayn baruf, / rozhinkes mit mandlen. / shlof-zhe, yidele, shlof.
Under Yidele's cradle / Stands a little clear-white goat. / The little goat has traveled to trade [his wares]. / This will be your job, too. / [Trading] raisins and almonds, / Sleep now, Yidele, sleep.

1936, Yiddle with His Fiddle (film)
איבער פֿעלדער וועגן אויף אַ וואָגן היי / מיט ווינט און זון און רעגן פֿאָרן קלעזמער צוויי
iber felder vegn oyf a vogn hey / mit vint un zun un regn forn klezmer tsvey
Traveling over fields on a wagon of hay, / In wind and sun and rain ride two klezmorim.

glosses: to ride, drive, travel (to go by vehicle or animal)

From Hebrew שָׁחַט (shakhát).
The pronunciation of the stem is likely to come from an older West Yiddish pronunciation where ח was pronounced /h/, causing the qamatz and patch to be pronounced with an e-like sound. The modern pronunciation comes from a /ht/ → /xt/ sound shift.

etymology_text:
A combination of the Middle High German forms of ־יק (-ik) and ־הייט (-heyt). Compare German -keit.
Unlike for ־הייט (-heyt), the Litvish pronunciation anomalously shifted to ־קײַט (-kayt).

etymology_text: From דער־ (der-) + ציילן (tseyln). Compare Bavarian derzöhn, German erzählen, Dutch vertellen.

examples.text: די חדר־יינגלעך האָבן עס גלייך געזען און דערציילט וועגן דעם זייערע עלטערן, אָבער די עלטערן האָבן זיך נישט געמאַכט דערפֿון, וואָס קינדער רעדן, און ווייטער געלאָזט די דערציאונג פֿון זײערע זיך אונטער דער השגחה פֿון אַ קראַנקן מענטשן.
examples.ref: 1946, I.J. Singer, “אַ ייד אַ מלמד פֿאַרגלוסט זיך צו ווערן אַ מלאך אום פּורים און פֿאַרלירט, נעבעך, אַן אויג”, in Fun a velt vos iz nishto mer:
examples.english: The heder kids saw it immediately and related this to their parents, but the parents didn't care what kids said, and so left the education of theirs under the care of a sick man.
examples.roman: di kheyder-yingelekh hobn es glaykh gezen un dertseylt vegn dem zeyere eltern, ober di eltern hobn zikh nisht gemakht derfun, vos kinder redn, un vayter gelozt di dertsiung fun zeyere zikh unter der hazhgokhe fun a krankn mentshn.
examples.translation: The heder kids saw it immediately and related this to their parents, but the parents didn't care what kids said, and so left the education of theirs under the care of a sick man.

examples.text:
איין שוואַרצע ייִדישע מאַמע האָט מיר דערציילט, אַז ווען זי האָט איין מאָל געבראַכט איר קינד צו אַן אונטערנעמונג פֿאַר ייִדישע קינדער, האָט זי פּלוצלינג דערהערט די פֿראַגע: „פֿאַר וואָס איז די גויע דאָ?‟
eyn shvartse yidishe mame hot mir dertseylt, az ven zi hot eyn mol gebrakht ir kind tsu an unternemung far yidishe kinder, hot zi plutsling derhert di frage: „far vos iz di goye do?‟
examples.ref: The Yiddish Forward, 22 July 2015
examples.english: One black Jewish mother told me that when she once brought her kid to an event for Jewish children, she suddenly heard the question, “Why is the goy here?”

etymology_text: From earlier various *גרימזיל״ש (*grimzils), *וורימזייל״ש (*vrimzils), *ברימזיל״ש pl (*frimzils) (12th century), ultimately from Vulgar Latin *vermicellus (“vermicelli”), alteration of vermiculus (“small worm”), from vermis (“worm”). First re-analyzed as suffixed with ־ל (-l) (attested as *וורמ״זליך (*frimzlikh)) in the second half of the 12th century, hence the neuter gender and diminutive plural. Emergence of *כר־ (*khr-) is attributed to the carryover of Slavic-origin consonant clusters. For the k-kh alternation between Western and Eastern Yiddish, compare כריין (khreyn).

etymology_text:
From Proto-Slavic *xrěnъ (“horseradish”), possibly via Old Czech chřěn. Note however also East Central German Krên, southern German Kren, also ultimately from the Proto-Slavic term.
In terms of Western Yiddish variants, given the lack of a diphthong, קרען (kren) was most likely directly borrowed from German, while קריין (kreyn) is likely to have been inherited naturally from Middle High German krên, krêne, chrên.
It is possible that the modern dominant Eastern Yiddish term was formed initially as קריין (kreyn), but later altered and re-converged with Slavic under the influence of contact Slavic languages; compare Polish chrzan, Russian хрен (xren).
For another case of k-kh alternation between Western and Eastern Yiddish, compare כרעמזל (khremzl).

glosses: chrain (a relish made principally from horseradish)

אַזוי ווי דער רבי האָט געזאָגט די דאָזיקע ווערטער, האָט ער זיך געטאָן אַ שטעל־אויף און אַ געשרײַ געטאָן: אין הימל האָב איך נישט קיין דעה, נאָר בײַ מיר אין בית מדרש האָב איך יאָ. פֿון הײַנט אָן און ווײַטער וועט בײַ מיר זײַן יעדער טאָג יום כיפּור – יעדער טאָג, אַחוץ שבת און יום־טוב.
azoy vi der rebe hot gezogt di dozike verter, hot er zikh geton a shtel-oyf un a geshray geton: in himl hob ikh nisht keyn deye, nor bay mir in bezmedresh hob ikh yo. fun haynt on un vayter vet bay mir zayn yeder tog yonkiper – yeder tog, akhuts shabes un yontef.
As the rabbi said these words, he stood up and yelled: In Heaven, I have no say; but in my synagogue I do. From today on, every day will be the Day of Atonement - every day, except for Sabbath and holidays.

examples.text:
Rozhinkes mit Mandlen (Yiddish folk lullaby):
אונטער ייִדעלע׳ס וויגעלע / שטייט אַ קלאָר־ווײַס ציגעלע. / דאָס ציגעלע איז געפֿאָרן האַנדלען. / דאָס וועט זײַן דײַן באַרוף, / ראָזשינקעס מיט מאַנדלען. / שלאָף־זשע, ייִדעלע, שלאָף.
unter yidele's vigele / shteyt a klor-vays tsigele. / dos tsigele iz geforn handlen. / dos vet zayn dayn baruf, / rozhinkes mit mandlen. / shlof-zhe, yidele, shlof.
Under Yidele's cradle / Stands a little clear-white goat. / The little goat has traveled to trade [his wares]. / This will be your job, too. / [Trading] raisins and almonds, / Sleep now, Yidele, sleep.

etymology_text: From Middle High German wellen, from Old High German wellen, and thus originally the same word as וועלן (veln, “to want”). The discrepant conjugations may be simple alternative forms grammaticalized in the pattern of the auxiliary. The Middle High German verb had -i- in the singular forms and -e- in the plural. Compare also in Middle High German the attested contraction witt for wilt (2nd person singular), and in later dialectal German willt for will (3rd person singular). However, a conflation with forms of ווערן (vern, “to become”) seems very likely. Both verbs (wellen and werden) were used to form the future tense in late Middle High German.

glosses: Auxiliary verb which puts the following verb in the future tense

examples.ref: 1894, שלום־עליכם (sholem-aleyhkem, “Sholem Aleichem”), “דאָס גרויסע געווינס (dos groyse gevins)”, in טבֿיה דער מילכיקער (tevye der milkhiker, “Tevye the Dairyman”):
examples.english: I have examined this from itself alone really, how thus has the Almighty dealt with me, with my current line of work: because how entirely do I suddenly come to sell cheese and butter, if my grandmother's grandmother had never peddled any dairy products? It's truly worthwhile that you should hear out the whole story from beginning to end.

etymology_text:
Following Šapiro, Russian etymological dictionaries (e.g. Preobraženskij, Vasmer) usually derive from לײַב (layb, “body”) (which in Poland was pronounced [laːp] and supposedly had a dialectal meaning “upper body garment”) and Polish serdak, Ukrainian серда́к (serdák, “a kind of men's outer garments”). Taking the meaning “torn clothes, rags” found in Belarusian to be the primary one, Preobraženskij offers an alternative derivation from German Lappen (“rag, cloth”) and Russian серту́к (sertúk), сюрту́к (sjurtúk, “frock coat”).
Perixanjan dismisses the above as folk etymologies and sees the origin in Persian لسپردرک (laspardarak, “handkerchief”), itself borrowed from Sogdian ܕܣܦܪܛܪ (dsprtr /⁠*ẟaspartar⁠/, “handkerchief”), through a sp → ps metathesis and haplology. She explains the arrival of the Iranian word into Eastern European Yiddish by Khazar mediation. The commercial links of Khazars with Iran and Central Asia are well-known.

Yiddish רוקן
From Middle High German rucke, variant of rücke, from Old High German rucki, from Proto-Germanic *hrugjaz. Lack of umlaut before a velar geminate is a southern, especially south-eastern German development (compare Bavarian Ruckn, Rucka). The dialectal basis of Yiddish is East Central German with a Bavarian influence.

etymology_text:
Perhaps from Middle High German ieman(d)s, originally genitive of ieman (“somebody”), but since the 15th century also attested as basic form. The suffix -er would have been added by analogy with the pronominal/adjectival declension (as also happened in the oblique cases of cognate German jemand); /n/ was lost by dissimilation.
Alternatively from Middle High German (ich) enweiz wer (“I don’t know who”), a common construction expressing indefiniteness, also reduced to neiz wer. Compare Alemannic German neiwer. For the construction see also Old Norse nǫkkurr and Romanian niște. The /m/ would be due to assimilation of -nw-, but the /ts/ (instead of /s/) is difficult to explain with this approach.

examples.text: פֿאַרװאָס־זשע קאָן איך ניט ענטפֿערען אױף דער אַנדערער פֿראַגע: „װאָס הײסט אײגענטום?“ – „עס איז גנבֿה“, און האָבען די זיכערקײט, אַז מען װעט מיך תיכף פֿערשטעהן, כאָטש דער צװיטער זאַץ איז דאָס אײגענע װאָס דער ערשטער נאָר אַביסעל איבערגעניצעװעט?
examples.ref: 1917, Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, chapter 1, in A. Koralnik, transl., װאָס איז אײגענטום? (vos iz eygentum?), page 29:
examples.english: So why can I not answer the other question, "What is property?" "It is theft," and be sure that people will immediately understand, even though the second sentence is the same as the first, only a little revamped?
examples.roman: farvos-zhe kon ikh nit entferen oyf der anderer frage: „vos heyst eygentum?“ – „es iz gneyve“, un hoben di zikherkeyt, az men vet mikh teykef fershten, khotsh der tsviter zats iz dos eygene vos der ershter nor abisel ibergenitsevet?
examples.translation: So why can I not answer the other question, "What is property?" "It is theft," and be sure that people will immediately understand, even though the second sentence is the same as the first, only a little revamped?

examples.text: זעליק האָט געהאָט דעם מאָנאָפּאָל אױף געשמוגלטן טאַבאַק פֿון ליטע; אַחוץ דעם איז ער געװען אַ גלאַװנער פּאַסער, דער אָפּנעמער פֿון יעדער גנבֿה איז שטאָט.
examples.ref: 1994, די גאָלדענע קייט (di goldene keyt):
examples.english: Zelik had a monopoly on smuggled tobacco from Lithuania; apart from this he was a major stolen goods dealer; the purchaser of every theft is the city government.
examples.roman: zelik hot gehot dem monopol oyf geshmugltn tabak fun lite; akhuts dem iz er geven a glavner paser, der opnemer fun yeder gneyve iz shtot.
examples.translation: Zelik had a monopoly on smuggled tobacco from Lithuania; apart from this he was a major stolen goods dealer; the purchaser of every theft is the city government.

examples.text: די גנבֿה פֿון דער אָרטאָדאָקסישער שיל, „יאָנג איזרעאַל אָוו מאָשאָלו פּאַרקוויי“, אויף איסט 208טער גאַס, איז אַנטדעקט געוואָרן דורך אַ שיל־אַרבעטער דעם פֿאַרגאַנגענעם זונטיק.
examples.ref: 2013 February 13, Sara-Rachel Shechter, “אַ גרויסער קלאַפּ פֿאַר אַ בראָנקסער שיל (a groyser klap far a bronkser shil) [Terrible Blow for a Bronx Shul]”, in Der Forverts:
examples.english: This theft from the Orthodox shul "Young Israel of Mosholu Parkway", on East 208th Street, was discovered by a synagogue worker this past Sunday.
examples.roman: di gneyve fun der ortodoksisher shil, „yong izreal ov mosholu parkvey“, oyf ist 208ter gas, iz antdekt gevorn durkh a shil-arbeter dem fargangenem zuntik.
examples.translation: This theft from the Orthodox shul "Young Israel of Mosholu Parkway", on East 208th Street, was discovered by a synagogue worker this past Sunday.

etymology_text:
From Polish żłób (“manger, trough; furrow, large groove in the soil”).
Originated in klezmer musician cant (Klezmer-loshn). The nature of the semantic shift from "manger, crib" to "boorish goy" remains unclear. In any case, by the year 1869, it had become common enough to be included in a Russian-Yiddish dictionary published in Zhytomyr. Jewish immigrants brought the word to the United States, where it is best known under the form schlub. In the Russosphere, the word жлоб (žlob) spread seemingly through criminal slang, which is considerably influenced by Odessan.
In its original sense, the word only applied to non-Jewish males. Strom (2002) lists "zhlobukhe-elzet" as a synonym, "zhlobevke" and "zlobike" (זלאָביקע) as female counterparts.

examples.ref: 1946, I.J. Singer, “אַ ייד אַ מלמד פאַרגלוסט זיך צו ווערן אַ מלאך אום פּורים און פאַרלירט, נעבעך, אַן אויג”, in Fun a velt vos iz nishto mer:
examples.english: Every term anew, during the intermediary period of Sukkot or the intermediary period of Pesach, I was very confident about being taken from one melamed and given to another, believing the new one would be better than the old.
examples.roman: yedn zman oyfsnay, khalemoyed sukes oder khalemoyed peysekh, bin ikh geven zeyer hoferdik, vos men hot mikh genumen eyn melamed un ongedungen tsu an andern, gleybndik, az der neyer vet zayn beser vi der alter.
examples.translation: Every term anew, during the intermediary period of Sukkot or the intermediary period of Pesach, I was very confident about being taken from one melamed and given to another, believing the new one would be better than the old.

examples.text: יעדן זמן אויפסניי, חול־המועד סוכות אָדער חול־המועד פּסח, בין איך געווען זייער האָפערדיק, וואָס מען האָט מיך גענומען איין מלמד און אָנגעדונגען צו אַן אַנדערן, גלײבנדיק, אַז דער נייער וועט זיין בעסער ווי דער אַלטער. יעדעם מאָל אויפסניי האָב איך זיך אַנטוישט אין מיינע האָפענונגען.
examples.ref: 1946, I.J. Singer, “אַ ייד אַ מלמד פאַרגלוסט זיך צו ווערן אַ מלאך אום פּורים און פאַרלירט, נעבעך, אַן אויג”, in Fun a velt vos iz nishto mer:
examples.english: Every term anew, during the intermediary period of Sukkot or the intermediary period of Pesach, I was very hopeful about being taken from one melamed and given to another, believing the new one would be better than the old. Every time anew, my hopes were let down.
examples.roman: yedn zman oyfsnay, khalemoyed sukes oder khalemoyed peysekh, bin ikh geven zeyer hoferdik, vos men hot mikh genumen eyn melamed un ongedungen tsu an andern, gleybndik, az der nayer vet zayn beser vi der alter. yedem mol oyfsnay hob ikh zikh antoysht in mayne hofenungen.
examples.translation: Every term anew, during the intermediary period of Sukkot or the intermediary period of Pesach, I was very hopeful about being taken from one melamed and given to another, believing the new one would be better than the old. Every time anew, my hopes were let down.

etymology_text: From Old High German kruzigōn, equivalent to קרייץ (kreyts, “cross”) + ־יק (-ik) + ־ן (-n).

examples.text: דאָס איז שוין ניט מער די שנאה, וואָס באַשולדיקט דעם אידן אין קרייציקן דעם קריסטוס, אין פאַרגיפטן קוואַלן, אין געברויכן קריסטלאַכע בלוט אויף פּסח.
examples.ref: 1927, Morris Winchevsky, געזאמלטע ווערק [Compiled Works], New York, page 264:
examples.english: This is no longer merely the hatred which accuses the Jew of crucifying the Christ, of poisoning wells, of using Christian blood for Passover.
examples.roman: dos iz shoyn nit mer di síne, vos bashúldikt dem idn in kréytsikn dem krístus, in fargíftn kvaln, in gebróykhn krístlakhe blut oyf péysekh.
examples.translation: This is no longer merely the hatred which accuses the Jew of crucifying the Christ, of poisoning wells, of using Christian blood for Passover.

examples.text: עס האָט ניט געקענט אָפּגעלייקנט ווערן דער פאַקט אַז יעזוס איז געקרייציקט געוואָרן דורך רוימישע סאָלדאַטן אויפן באַפעל פון פּילאַטוסן: האָט מען אָנגענומען דעם לעצטן מיטל אַז די יידן האָבן געצוווּנגען פּילאַטוסן צו קרייציקן יעזוסן.
examples.ref: 1958, Abbo Ostrowsky, פירוש [commentary], page 416:
examples.english: The fact that Jesus was crucified by Roman soldiers at the command of Pilate could not be denied; therefore, the last resort was adopted: that the Jews forced Pilate to crucify Jesus.
examples.roman: es hot nit geként ópgeléyknt vern der fakt az yézus iz gekréytsikt gevórn durkh róymishe soldátn oyfn bafél fun pilátusn: hot men óngenumen dem letstn mitl az di yidn hobn getsvúngen pilátusn tsu kréytsikn yézusn.
examples.translation: The fact that Jesus was crucified by Roman soldiers at the command of Pilate could not be denied; therefore, the last resort was adopted: that the Jews forced Pilate to crucify Jesus.

examples.text: די הויפּט־שׂינאה האָט זיך אַנטוויקלט אין דעם יאָרטויזנט אַרום קרייציקן דעם ענין פֿון ישו, דעם זון פֿון גאָט, דורך זײַנע ברידער, די ייִדן.
examples.ref: 2004, David S. Katz, אַשכּנז [Ashkenazi], →ISBN, page 139:
examples.english: The primary hatred developed over the millennium around the crucifixion of the matter of Jesus, the Son of God, by his brothers, the Jews.
examples.roman: di hoypt-síne hot zikh antvíklt in dem yortóyznt arúm kréytsikn dem ínyen fun yéyshu, dem zun fun got, durkh záyne bríder, di yidn.
examples.translation: The primary hatred developed over the millennium around the crucifixion of the matter of Jesus, the Son of God, by his brothers, the Jews.

glosses: to crucify (to execute via nailing to a cross)

etymology_text: Probably borrowed from Old French Bonhomme. Bonhomme is a family name in France to this day and goes back to the Middle Ages (it turns up in England as Bonham as early as 1327); "bon nom", on the other hand, could be a calque of the Hebrew name שם טוב (shem tov), which reached southern France from Spain, as in the family of the 13th-century Provençal philosopher Shem-Tov ibn Falaquera. And if Bunim comes from "bon nom", it is actually a calque of a calque, since Shem Tov is a Hebraization of the Greek name Kalonymos, which appears in the Talmud, surfaces again in eighth-century Italy, belonging to a renowned Jewish family in the medieval Rhineland and eventually became the Eastern European Kalman.

etymology_text: From Middle High German zedele, zedel, a loan from Italian cedola, from Medieval Latin cedula, schedula, the diminutive of scheda, scida (“strip of papyrus”) ultimately from Ancient Greek σχίδη (skhídē, “splinter, fragment”). Cognate to Low German Zeddel, Palatine Rhine Franconian Zeddel, English schedule. Compare German Zettel m, which likely also influenced the spelling (as opposed to *צעדל (*tsedl)). The neuter gender derives from a re-interpretation of the word, as if it was suffixed by ־ל (-l), hence also the plural form צעטלעך (tsetlekh).

From Russian шма́ра (šmára, “prostitute”) + вози́ть (vozítʹ, “to carry, to transport”) + -ник (-nik). It is formed in a humorous way, based on other words ending in -возник (-voznik), such as навозник (navoznik, “dung transporter”) and парово́зный (parovóznyj, “locomotive”) + -ник (-nik), since it rhymes.
Alternatively, from Middle High German smirn, from older smirwen, from Old High German smirwen, from Proto-West Germanic *smirwijan, from Proto-Germanic *smirwijaną (“to smear, to anoint”).

examples.translation: “Why must you be against this? We'll provide him with good room and board; in the middle of the week, he'll eat in the yeshiva's kitchen together with other students and on Shabbat we'll send him to eat at a nice home.”

examples.text: זעלדע און די יינגסטע טאָכטער שטייען ביי קוישן אויבס, די מיטלסטע טאָכטער פאַרקויפט אַלערליי גרינסן, און די עלטסטע טאָכטער, די גרעסטע בראַנד, שטייט ביי קעסטלעך מיט געטרינקטע פישעלעך, ביי אַ טון מיט שמאַלץ־הערינג, ביי סלאָיען געזייערטע אוגערקעס.

examples.english: Zelda and her youngest daughter stood by baskets of fruit, the middle daughter sold all kinds of greens, and the eldest daughter, the greatest shrieker, stood by boxes of dried out fish, the barrel of shmaltz herring, and by jars of pickles.
examples.roman: zelde un di yingste tokhter shteyen bay koyshn oybs, di mitlste tokhter farkoyft alerley grinsn, un di eltste tokhter, di greste brand, shteyt bay kestlekh mit getrinkte fishelekh, bay a tun mit shmalts-hering, bay sloyen gezeyerte ugerkes.
examples.translation: Zelda and her youngest daughter stood by baskets of fruit, the middle daughter sold all kinds of greens, and the eldest daughter, the greatest shrieker, stood by boxes of dried out fish, the barrel of shmaltz herring, and by jars of pickles.

etymology_text: Ultimately from English kangaroo, from Guugu Yimidhirr gangurru (“eastern grey kangaroo”).

examples.text: דער קענגורו בּאַוואוינט די העלע שיטערע וועלדלעך און די סטעפּנדיקע פּליינען פֿון אַווסטראַליע.
examples.ref: 1921, Otto Shmeyl, זאָאָלאָגיע [Zoology], Vilnius: Shul Farlag, page 53:
examples.english: The kangaroo inhabits the bright sparce woods and the steppelike planes of Australia.
examples.roman: der kenguru bavoynt di hele shitere veldlekh un di stepndike pleynen fun avstralye.
examples.translation: The kangaroo inhabits the bright sparce woods and the steppelike planes of Australia.

examples.text: ער האָט זיך אַוועקגעזעצט אַף די הינטערשטע פיסלאך, זיך אָנגעשפּארט אַפן וויידעלע, פּונקט ווי אַ קליינער קענגורו, און האָט זיך ארומגעקוקט אין אלע זייטן און עפּעס געבורטשעט.
examples.ref: 1924, Rudyard Kipling, chapter II, in ריקי־טיקי־טאווי [Riki-Tiki-Tavi], Kiev: Kultur-Lige, page 14:
examples.english: He stood up on his tiny back paws, leaned on his tail, just like a small kangaroo, and looked around to all sides and grumbled something.
examples.roman: er hot zikh avekgezetst af di hintershte fislakh, zikh ongeshpart afn veydele, punkt vi a kleyner kenguru, un hot zikh arumgekukt in ale zaytn un epes geburtshet.
examples.translation: He stood up on his tiny back paws, leaned on his tail, just like a small kangaroo, and looked around to all sides and grumbled something.

examples.text: דאָרט אין וואַלד, אַ ייִדיש ביידל, / און עס גרינט אין גאַנצן לאַנד. / זיפֿצט אין אַלקערל אַ מיידל / מיטן פּנים צו דער וואַנט. / „וואָס איז מיידל, דײַן פֿאַרלאַנגען? / ס׳איז אַ שאָד אַ יעדער טרערן“ / „דער וואָס איז אַוועקגעגאַנגען, / וועט צו איך נישט קומען מער.“

examples.roman: dort in vald, a yidish beydl, / un es grint in gantsn land. / ziftst in alkerl a meydl / mitn ponem tsu der vant. / „vos iz meydl, dayn farlangen? / s'iz a shod a yeder trern“ / „der vos iz avekgegangen, / vet tsu ikh nisht kumen mer.“
examples.translation: In the forest, a Jewish hut, / and all the land's in bloom. / A girl sighs in her room, / with her face to the wall. / "What is, girl, your desire? / It's a shame, every tear." / "He who is departed, / will return no more."

categories.name: Yiddish entries with incorrect language header

examples.text: בעת ער האָט ביים שפּאַצירן דערזען אַ חברה יינגערע, איז ער שטיין געבליבן און געוואַרט ביז די חברה איז אים פאַרבייגעגאַנגען, אַ זייטיקער זאָל ניט מיינען אַז ער איז איינער פון די אָנהייבער פאַרזיכניקעס.
examples.ref: 1967, Chaim Grade, צמח אַטלאַס [Tsemakh Atlas], volume 1, page 200:
examples.english: While walking, if he spotted a group of younger students, he would stay still and wait until the group passed him so that an onlooker wouldn't think he was one of those beginning to study independently.
examples.roman: beys er hot baym shpatsirn derzen a khevre yingere, iz er shteyn geblibn un gevart biz di khevre iz im farbaygegangen, a zaytiker zol nit meynen az er iz eyner fun di onheyber farzikhnikes.
examples.translation: While walking, if he spotted a group of younger students, he would stay still and wait until the group passed him so that an onlooker wouldn't think he was one of those beginning to study independently.

glosses: someone who works alone, an independent

head_templates.name: yi-noun
head_templates.expansion: צדיק גמור • (tsadek gomer) m, plural צדיקים גמורים (tsadikim gmurim), feminine צדיקת גמורה (tsadeykes gmure)

etymology_text: From צדיק (tsadik, “tzaddik, righteous person”) + גמור (gomer, “whole, entire”)

examples.text: יענער האָט דערציילט אַנדערע און מען האָט גענומען טרייבן פון אים קאַטאָוועס. „מה רעש, ר׳ יואל, אַז די כלה איז אַ טויבלעכע? געווען צדיקים גמורים וואָס האָבן געזוכט אַ ווייב דווקא אַ טויב־שטומע, זי זאָל ניט קענען הערן און ריידן לשן־הרע.“

examples.translation: “Before we say the Shema and lie down to sleep, we ask each other for forgiveness. We don't want someone to go to sleep with a grudge against a friend and so we ask each other for forgiveness.”

examples.text: צוויי טויזנט יאָר האָט מען אונז באמת געקרייציקט צוליבן בילבול וועגן יענער קרייציקונג — בעת די קרייצצוגן און במשך פון אונזער צוויי טויזנט־יאָריקער מאַרטירער־געשיכטע בכלל.
examples.ref: 1958, Eliyahu-Khayim Sheps, שלום אַש, אַ סך־הכּל [Sholem Asch, a Final Reckoning], אונדזער וועג, page 16:
examples.english: For two thousand years we were really crucified because of the confusion about that crucifixion — during the crusades and during our two thousand year history of martyrdom in general.
examples.roman: tsvey toyznt yor hot men unz beémes gekréytsikt tsulíbn bilbl vegn yéner kréytsikung — beys di kréytstsugn un beméshekh fun unzer tsvey toyznt-yóriker martírer-geshíkhte bikhlál.
examples.translation: For two thousand years we were really crucified because of the confusion about that crucifixion — during the crusades and during our two thousand year history of martyrdom in general.

examples.text: פֿאַר די פּאָדלע זשידעס איז אָבער ווייניק נאָר דאָס בלוט פֿונעם אויסלייזער, וועלכן זיי האָבן געקרייציקט.
examples.ref: 2004, Boris Sandler, ווען דער גולם האָט פֿאַרמאַכט די אויגן [When the Golem Closed his Eyes], Leyvik House, page 178:
examples.english: For the vile kikes, however, even the blood of the Redeemer, whom they crucified, is not enough.
examples.roman: far di pódle zhídes iz óber véynik nor dos blut fúnem óysleyzer, velkhn zey hobn gekréytsikt.
examples.translation: For the vile kikes, however, even the blood of the Redeemer, whom they crucified, is not enough.

etymology_text:
Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *pel-
Proto-Indo-European *-ti
Proto-Indo-European *pl(e)h₂-n-g-e-tider.
Proto-Italic *plāngō
Latin plangōder.
Yiddish פּלאַנכען
Ultimately from Latin plangō, although specific Romance intermediate uncertain. According to one theory, a borrowing from Old Occitan, the ancestor of modern Occitan plànher, seems most likely, first borrowed as the Western Yiddish form, which then shifted from [planj-] → [planç-] → [planx-] as the present form, which then spread to almost all Yiddish varieties. Theories that the term derives from a French or Italian intermediate are less likely, but cannot be ruled out.
